description:
Gurdwara Pehli Patshahi, popularly called Jind Pir, stands on the Sukkur side of the great bridge that carries the Lahore–Karachi railway across the Indus between Sukkur and Rohri. By tradition it marks a spot graced by Guru Nanak, the first Guru (*Pehli Patshahi*), during his third journey (*udasi*) through Sindh; it was from here, the tradition holds, that he crossed to the river islet later famous as Sadh Belo (a separate entry in this dataset). Its first custodian is said to have been an Udasi *sadhu* of the Jhulelal devotion, and the shrine passed into the keeping of the Nanakpanthi community of Sindh — Hindus and Sikhs together — who honour Guru Nanak without a firm confessional boundary. Within, the *Guru Granth Sahib* is installed and its *prakash* performed, while images are also venerated, and a lamp said to have been kindled by the Guru himself is kept burning day and night, before which pilgrims bow. The gurdwara is thus a characteristic monument of Sindh's syncretic Nanakpanthi tradition, distinct both from the island temple of Sadh Belo and from the other Sikh sites of the Sukkur–Rohri conurbation. Much of its detailed history survives only in oral and community tradition. Independent, gazetteer-derived scholarship attests that the name "Zinda Pir" (or "Jinda Pir") also belongs to an older riverine shrine at Sukkur, at which Hindus and Muslims worshipped jointly until the late nineteenth century, when — per the 1919 Gazetteer of Sindh — the Hindu congregation "abandoned their claim and set up a shrine of their own to Jinda Pir on the Sukkur bank"; whether that shrine and this Sikh gurdwara are the same structure, two structures sharing one name, or otherwise related is not established by any source consulted, and neither account confirms the other.

## Bibliography
- Iqbal Qaiser, *Historical Sikh Shrines in Pakistan* (Lahore: Punjabi History Board, 1998), p. 120.
- Alice Albinia, "Life Around The Indus: Tracing River Worship In Sindh," *Outlook Traveller*, 30 September 2014.
qa_note: Open question, not resolved: Iqbal Qaiser's *Historical Sikh Shrines in Pakistan* places this gurdwara ("Gurdwara Pehli Patshahi, Jind Pir") on the Sukkur side of the bridge, in Nanakpanthi Hindu keeping. Alice Albinia's account (via the 1874 and 1919 Gazetteers of Sindh, in *Outlook Traveller*, 2014) independently describes a similarly-named "Zinda Pir"/"Jinda Pir" shrine on an Indus islet at Sukkur, historically shared by Hindus and Muslims, with the Hindu congregation later founding a shrine of their own on the Sukkur bank — geographically consistent with where Qaiser places the gurdwara, but Albinia's account makes no mention of Sikhs, Guru Nanak, or a gurdwara at all. Whether the two sources describe the same physical site is unresolved and reported here rather than decided. This addition rests on a single independently-verified source for the gurdwara itself (Qaiser) and has not yet been corroborated by a second source that confirms the Sikh gurdwara specifically.
